1.pericope_label: The Lord reigneth: robed, girded, enthroned of old

schools.summary: Augustine takes the supplied title seriously: the sixth day is meant, on which the animals were made and last of all man in God's likeness, and the order was not arbitrary, since the ages were to run a like course before we rest in God — but we rest only if we do good works, God having rested on the seventh day not from weariness, nor having left off working, since our Lord says his Father worketh hitherto.

Calvin keeps the confession where it does its work: our failure to invest God with the power belonging to him is the source of the fear we so often feel, and though all admit in word that God reigns, few oppose that shield to the hostile powers of the world. Gill reads the whole of the King Messiah, set up from everlasting and one day to reign manifestly, and takes the throne established of old for one prepared from eternity.

Henry calls God's dominion the thing we are most concerned to believe next to his being, and measures the majesty by contrast — that of earthly princes beside God's is a glow-worm's glimmering beside the sun going forth in his strength; Spurgeon hears a throne briefly seeming vacant, the Lord on a sudden putting on his regal apparel and ascending his lofty seat, and insists he is clothed not with emblems of majesty but with majesty itself.

Clarke reports that neither Hebrew nor Chaldee gives the psalm a title, that the versions which supply one carry no information a man can rely on, and that twelve manuscripts write it as part of the psalm before; he thinks it written at the close of the captivity by Levites. Wesley says the majesty and strength God always had he will now show in the eyes of all people.

Ellicott renders the opening 'Jehovah has become king', the usual term for ascending a throne, and reads the robing and girding as part of an inauguration, the clauses running better as 'majesty he has put on'; Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm among those beholding the perfected theocracy as the appearing of Jahve himself rather than of a human king, a series parallel with the christocratic psalms that converges but never meets in the Old Testament.

debates.question: How should the opening words be rendered?

sides.position: 'Jehovah has become king' — the usual idiom for ascending a throne, with robing and girding as inauguration
a statement of continuous government — he continues to rule all he has created

3.pericope_label: The floods lift up their voice

schools.summary: Gill answers the question by naming the enemies: Christ is the most High, mightier than all his foes and the noise they make — stronger than the strong man armed, than Satan and his principalities, than the persecuting princes of this world, than antichrist, yea than the mighty waves; and on the testimonies he sets aside the works of nature and the Scriptures themselves in favour of the promises, especially those respecting the kingdom.

Clarke takes the floods at once for men, troop succeeding troop as the waves succeed each other, and holds that the most powerful empires prevail nothing; on the closing verse he writes at most length, widening the holiness that becomes God's house to building, ministers, members, ordinances, faith, discipline and practice, and passing on the old Psalter's reading that the house of God is man's soul. Wesley takes the testimonies for promises concerning the Messiah's kingdom.

Ellicott leaves it doubtful whether the raging sea is literal or emblematic of war, prefers 'roaring' to 'waves' for the parallelism, and notes that repeating the verb a third time in a different tense adds force; he ties the testimonies closely to the verse before, the permanence of the covenant proving the divine power superior to the forces of nature.

debates.question: Are the floods literal seas or hostile nations?

sides.position: nations — multitudes confederated against God’s people
doubtful; the description may be literal or emblematic of war and its horrors
